The [prior-predictive page](prior-predictive-distributions.qmd) averaged the observation model over the prior. A **posterior predictive distribution** averages over the posterior. The Turkish UniMorph example also lets us compare that counterfactual independent-draw prediction with the actual without-replacement design.

## Prediction under the exchangeable Bernoulli model

For one future binary value,

$$
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde Z=1\mid\mathbf z)
=
\int_0^1\theta
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\,\mathrm d\theta
=
\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z].
$$

For a future independent block of $m$ cells,

$$
\widetilde K\mid\Theta=\theta
\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(m,\theta),
$$

and a $\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha',\beta')$ posterior gives

$$
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r\mid\mathbf z)
=
\binom mr
\frac{B(r+\alpha',m-r+\beta')}{B(\alpha',\beta')}.
$$

Its expectation and variance are

$$
\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K\mid\mathbf z]
=m\frac{\alpha'}{\alpha'+\beta'},
$$

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K\mid\mathbf z]
=
m\frac{\alpha'\beta'}{(\alpha'+\beta')^2}
\frac{\alpha'+\beta'+m}{\alpha'+\beta'+1}.
$$

## Predicting from the known remaining resource

The actual committed sample removed its rows from the pinned resource. If another block is drawn without replacement from the remaining $N_r$ cells, of which $K_r$ are focal, then

$$
\mathbb{P}(\widetilde K=r\mid N_r,K_r,m)
=
\frac{\binom{K_r}{r}\binom{N_r-K_r}{m-r}}{\binom{N_r}{m}}.
$$

This hypergeometric distribution is not a posterior. It is the sampling distribution induced by the known finite resource.

```{r}
#| label: compute-unimorph-predictive-designs
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

N <- nrow(population)
K <- sum(population$t_initial)
n <- nrow(sample_120)
k <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)
N_remaining <- N - n
K_remaining <- K - k
m <- n

unit_count <- 1L
alpha_post <- unit_count + k
beta_post <- unit_count + n - k
support <- 0:m

posterior_mass <- exp(
  lchoose(m, support) +
    lbeta(support + alpha_post, m - support + beta_post) -
    lbeta(alpha_post, beta_post)
)
finite_mass <- dhyper(
  support, m = K_remaining,
  n = N_remaining - K_remaining, k = m
)

posterior_mean <- m * alpha_post / (alpha_post + beta_post)
posterior_variance <- m * alpha_post * beta_post *
  (alpha_post + beta_post + m) /
  ((alpha_post + beta_post)^2 * (alpha_post + beta_post + 1))
finite_mean <- m * K_remaining / N_remaining
finite_variance <- m * K_remaining / N_remaining *
  (1 - K_remaining / N_remaining) *
  (N_remaining - m) / (N_remaining - 1)

stopifnot(
  N == 588L, K == 200L, n == 120L, k == 42L,
  abs(sum(posterior_mass) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs(sum(finite_mass) - 1) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(
  design = c("posterior independent block", "remaining resource without replacement"),
  expected_count = c(posterior_mean, finite_mean),
  variance = c(posterior_variance, finite_variance),
  next_cell_probability = c(
    alpha_post / (alpha_post + beta_post),
    K_remaining / N_remaining
  )
)
```

The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model predicts a mean of `r sprintf("%.3f", posterior_mean)` *t*-initial rows and variance `r sprintf("%.3f", posterior_variance)`. The actual remaining-resource design has mean `r sprintf("%.3f", finite_mean)` and variance `r sprintf("%.3f", finite_variance)`. The difference is a design difference, not a small correction to one model.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-predictive-designs
#| fig-cap: "Predictive masses for a second 120-cell block. The posterior beta-binomial uses an independent-draw model; the narrower hypergeometric mass uses the known remaining finite population."
predictive <- rbind(
  data.frame(count = support, probability = posterior_mass,
             design = "posterior independent draws"),
  data.frame(count = support, probability = finite_mass,
             design = "known resource, no replacement")
)

ggplot(subset(predictive, probability > 1e-5),
       aes(count, probability, linetype = design)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "t-initial forms in a second 120-cell block",
       y = "Predictive probability", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Two sources of posterior-predictive variation

The law of total variance gives

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K\mid\mathbf z]
=
\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}[\widetilde K\mid\Theta,\mathbf z]\mid\mathbf z]
+
\operatorname{Var}[\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K\mid\Theta,\mathbf z]\mid\mathbf z].
$$

The first term averages binomial variation, while the second represents variation in the conditional mean $m\Theta$ across the posterior.

```{r}
#| label: decompose-unimorph-predictive-variance
theta_mean <- alpha_post / (alpha_post + beta_post)
theta_variance <- alpha_post * beta_post /
  ((alpha_post + beta_post)^2 * (alpha_post + beta_post + 1))
mean_conditional_variance <- m *
  (theta_mean * (1 - theta_mean) - theta_variance)
variance_conditional_mean <- m^2 * theta_variance

stopifnot(abs(mean_conditional_variance + variance_conditional_mean -
                posterior_variance) < 1e-10)
data.frame(mean_conditional_variance, variance_conditional_mean,
           total = posterior_variance)
```

More simulation draws can estimate either predictive distribution more precisely, but they do not reduce future variation. And neither distribution supports a token-frequency claim about Turkish.

## Check your understanding

1. Why does the one-cell exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model prediction equal the posterior mean?
2. Which term in total variance disappears under a plug-in prediction?
3. Why is the hypergeometric prediction narrower?
4. Which prediction matches another sample from the committed resource?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Conditional on $\Theta$, the success probability is $\Theta$; averaging it over the posterior gives $\mathbb{P}(\widetilde Z=1\mid\mathbf z)=\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The plug-in fixes $\Theta$, so $\operatorname{Var}[\mathbb{E}[\widetilde K\mid\Theta,\mathbf z]\mid\mathbf z]$, the parameter-uncertainty term, disappears. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Sampling without replacement uses up focal and nonfocal cells and adds a finite-population correction, reducing variance. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The hypergeometric prediction matches another without-replacement sample from the remaining committed resource. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
